overview: This atlas record joins imperial Japan before 1945 to postwar Japan from 1960 onward. The intervening occupation has a separate map record; Japan itself did not disappear. Imperial colonies and occupied societies had their own histories. The 1938 snapshot assigns Cambodia and Cochin China to Japan prematurely, while later outlines omit Okinawa. These shapes are not reliable year-by-year borders. This card follows political transformation and selected everyday experiences, without treating twentieth-century Japan as one unchanged empire.

periods.title: Imperial expansion and war
periods.summary: This map interval includes growing political repression and war across Asia and the Pacific.

periods.title: Defeat and occupation
periods.summary: Allied occupation transformed government and landholding; the atlas labels this interval separately.

periods.title: Postwar institutions and changing lives
periods.summary: Sovereignty returned in 1952; Okinawa remained under U.S. administration until 1972.

items.text: In January 1915, Japan presented China with twenty-one demands, seeking privileges in Shandong, Manchuria and elsewhere. China accepted a revised ultimatum in May after most of the final group of demands had been removed. Diplomatic pressure accompanied Japan’s expanding power.

The 1925 voting reform removed the tax qualification for male voters, but excluded people receiving public or private assistance. Women still could not vote. The same political bargain produced the anti-communist Peace Preservation Law: wider participation coexisted with stronger repression.

Japan’s expanding war in China included the mass killing of civilians at Nanjing in 1937. The December 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor widened the Pacific war. Military expansion brought occupation and suffering to neighboring societies, not simply a larger colored area on a map.

The atlas’s 1938 outline already includes features labeled Cambodia and Cochin China under Japan. Diplomatic records instead place Japanese demands for bases in southern Indochina in July 1941. A coarse snapshot can slide later events backward, so this map should not establish who controlled a particular town in 1938.

American atomic bombs devastated Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945. On 2 September, Japanese representatives signed the surrender aboard USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay. The surviving document records an enormous political break, while survivors and displaced families faced the work of rebuilding.

The U.S.-led Allied occupation ran from 1945 to 1952, although the map’s occupation label lasts until 1960. Occupation reforms redistributed agricultural land toward tenant farmers and reduced large landlords’ power. Political change could therefore alter who owned the field a family worked.

Women voted in the general election of 10 April 1946, and thirty-nine women won seats in the Diet. The National Diet Library preserves a campaign poster carrying words by writer Ikuta Hanayo encouraging women to vote. Political participation became visible in both polling places and printed messages.

The new constitution took effect on 3 May 1947. It located sovereignty in the people, made the emperor a symbol without governing powers, and renounced war as a means of settling international disputes. These provisions distinguish postwar institutions from the earlier imperial order.

A short Japanese sample is “個人の尊厳” (kojin no songen), “individual dignity.” It appears in Article 24 of the constitution promulgated in 1946, in the rules for laws on marriage and family. This is the library’s transcription; the romanized reading is supplied here. The article also specifies spouses’ equal rights.

The preserved Okawa house in Tokyo’s Den’enchofu suburb was built in 1925. Bedrooms, a dining room and a study surrounded the living room. Its entirely Western-style rooms were unusual at the time. One house reveals a family’s architectural choices without turning them into everybody’s standard home.

Kodakara-yu, a Tokyo public bathhouse built in 1929, had a grand curved gable, carvings of seven lucky gods and a decorative dressing-room ceiling. The preserved building makes a splendid reminder that washing could involve shared neighborhood spaces. Even a bathhouse could dress up for company.

Japan’s 1954 School Lunch Law established a national framework for meals, financing and support. Preparation standards covered kitchen equipment and nutritional content, and the program expanded to lower secondary schools in 1956. Feeding pupils required cooks, supplies and budgets as well as lunchboxes.

School health was another part of childhood. The 1958 School Health Law specified school physicians, dentists and pharmacists and their professional roles. A school could become a place for health checks as well as lessons, although the law alone does not prove identical services at every school.

About thirty million people still lacked medical insurance in 1956, according to the health ministry’s historical account. In 1961, expanded National Health Insurance brought farmers and self-employed people into universal coverage. It helped families manage medical bills; insurance coverage did not make every treatment free.

The same account describes a coordinated campaign against tuberculosis: antibiotics entered insurance coverage in 1950, followed by screening, BCG vaccination and visits from public-health nurses. Hospitals mattered, but schools, workplaces and homes also became places where disease prevention happened.

In 1958, Momofuku Ando developed Chicken Ramen in a small shed behind his home in Ikeda. Adding hot water turned the dried product into a quick meal. It is a kitchen invention with a pleasantly modest workshop: the famous noodles began without a grand laboratory.

UNESCO’s 2013 description of washoku highlights New Year preparations: pounding rice cakes, arranging symbolic foods and sharing dishes with relatives or neighbors. Special tableware and skills passed between generations make a meal a social occasion. These are documented traditions, not a menu followed identically by every family.

Toilets acquired their own engineering story. TOTO introduced its WASHLET warm-water cleansing seat in 1980, then a self-cleaning spray wand in 1983. A bathroom fitting could have moving parts and a design history! These are product milestones, not evidence that every household immediately owned one.

sections.title: Connections, local histories and living memory

items.text: The Tokaido Shinkansen opened on 1 October 1964, creating a high-speed rail connection on Japan’s main transport corridor. The operator’s 2024 report also stresses ordinary regional trains used for work and school. Famous express trains and everyday commuting belong to the same transport story.

Okinawa’s experience followed a different timetable. After the devastating 1945 battle, it remained under U.S. administration until 15 May 1972. Local history and Ryukyuan cultural traditions continued through these political changes. The later atlas outline’s omission of Okinawa must not erase the islands or their residents.

On 11 March 2011, the earthquake off northeastern Japan generated a devastating tsunami. Japan’s meteorological agency records that some observation stations stopped reporting because of tsunami damage, broken networks and power failures. Preserved measurements and accounts help explain both the disaster and the limits of instruments during it.

ending.text: Japan continued after the empire’s defeat, with transformed institutions under the postwar constitution. The atlas’s 1960 return to this label and its last stored 2020 boundary are mapping seams, not founding or disappearance dates.
